column3: The Hebrew shifts from plural houses to singular verbs and pronouns; BSB keeps the houses plural throughout.

The Hebrew calls the poor man “your brother” and says “his hand falters”; BSB says “your countryman” and interprets his condition as being unable to support himself.
The Hebrew calls the beneficiary “your brother”; BSB says “your countryman.”
The Hebrew repeats “give” for silver and food; BSB interprets the actions as “lend” and “sell.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls him “your brother” and uses passive “is sold to you”; BSB says “a countryman” and active “sells himself to you.”
The Hebrew says he shall “be with you” and “work with you”; BSB says “stay with you” and “work for you.”
The Hebrew says he and “his sons with him” shall “go out from you” and repeats the returning verb; BSB uses “his children,” passive “be released,” and one returning verb.
The Hebrew begins “they are My servants,” without repeating Israel’s name; BSB supplies “the Israelites.”
The Hebrew uses singular “him”; BSB says plural “them.”
The Hebrew uses singular “your male slave” and “your female slave” and repeats both nouns as the purchase objects; BSB uses plural “menservants and maidservants,” then “them.”
The Hebrew uses an active birth verb for those whom the resident families have begotten in the land; BSB uses passive “who are born in your land.”
The Hebrew gives the duration as “forever”; BSB says “for life.”
The Hebrew uses “hand” for prosperity, “your brother” for the poor man, and passive “is sold”; BSB says “prospers,” “your countryman,” and active “sells himself.”
The Hebrew uses passive “after he has been sold”; BSB says active “after he has sold himself.”

The Hebrew repeats the redeeming verb, names the cousin as “the son of his uncle,” and expresses prosperity through “his hand”; BSB states redeeming once for the relatives and uses “cousin” and “prospers.”
The Hebrew uses passive “his being sold” and refers to “the days of a hired worker”; BSB uses active “he sold himself” and specifies “daily wages.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says he shall “be with him” like a worker hired year by year and leaves the ruling subject as “he”; BSB uses passive “be treated” and supplies “a foreign owner.”
The Hebrew says “he and his sons with him” shall “go out”; BSB uses “his children” and passive “be released.”
Close to the Hebrew.
